messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Linh is a fifty-seven-year-old Vietnamese-American interior designer who has been married for nearly thirty years and, until recently, was regarded by colleagues as someone of extraordinary composure and creative precision. She presents with a PCL-5 score of 72, seeking help for the first time following what she describes as a "complete collapse" of her ability to function at work. The trauma that underlies her current presentation occurred approximately fourteen months ago, when she was attending a client event at a downtown hotel. A coordinated terrorist attack struck the venue mid-evening: there were explosions, a crush of panicked bodies, the smell of smoke and spilled alcohol from an overturned bar, and the sight of people bleeding on a marble floor she had herself designed. Linh was physically uninjured but was trapped for over two hours in a service corridor with several wounded strangers before emergency services reached them. It is the specific texture of that night — the reek of alcohol soaking into her clothes, the faces of people she did not know, the helplessness — that has never fully left her.

In the months that followed, Linh found that the world she returned to was no longer legible in the way it had been. She had come to believe, with quiet but absolute certainty, that the world is a dangerous place and that any environment can become lethal without warning. This conviction did not feel like a thought she could examine; it felt like a fact she had learned the hard way. Keeping constant watch over her surroundings seemed not paranoid but rational, and she began scanning every room she entered — restaurants, showrooms, her own studio — for people whose behaviour struck her as unusual or threatening. This hypervigilance was exhausting, but she was certain that relaxing it would cost her. What frightened her most was the corollary belief: that when something did go wrong, she would not be able to cope. Even minor frustrations — a supplier delay, a miscommunication with a client — now felt unsurvivable, confirming her fear that she had lost whatever resilience she once had.

It was this entrenched sense of threat and personal fragility that began to make ordinary triggers unbearable. Because she already moved through the world in a state of anticipated danger, any sensory echo of the attack arrived with the full force of the original. At a client lunch, a waiter spilled wine nearby, and the smell of alcohol hit her before she could prepare — her body responded as though the hotel corridor had reconstituted itself around her. She found herself suddenly feeling and acting as if the attack were happening again, gripping the table, unable to speak. Old photographs from her portfolio, which included images of the hotel's interior taken before the attack, became impossible to open on her computer. A colleague once touched her shoulder from behind to get her attention, and Linh reacted with such alarm that she knocked over her drafting tools and had to leave the room. Talking about the event, even obliquely with her husband, produced the same visceral flooding.

To manage these states, Linh developed a set of strategies that made sense to her at the time. She began pushing herself through punishing early-morning runs — sometimes two hours before work — telling herself that if she exhausted her body, her mind would quiet. When it did not, she ate compulsively in the evenings, not from hunger but to fill a space she could not name. And on the worst nights, when the flashbacks had been most vivid and her sense of herself as capable felt most shattered, she hurt herself physically — small, controlled injuries that she experienced as a release from feelings that otherwise had no exit. She told no one. Over time, however, these strategies began to compound her distress rather than contain it. The excessive exercise left her depleted and prone to injury, which reinforced her belief that her body, like her mind, was failing her. Waking sore and ashamed, she was more easily startled, more alert to threat in the faces of strangers, more convinced that she could not manage. The physical pain from self-harm occasionally triggered intrusive body memories of the attack, pulling her back into the very states she had been trying to escape. The cycle had become self-sealing.

Linh finally sought help after she was unable to complete a client walkthrough — a routine task she had performed hundreds of times — because the building's lobby bar produced an unmistakable smell of alcohol, and she froze completely in front of her client. She is most afraid that she will never recover the professional self she was. She is most hoping, she said quietly in the first session, simply to stop being frightened all the time.
